BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Iraq's government has authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to submit to Washington amendments to a draft security agreement with the United States, an Iraqi government spokesman said Tuesday. Students protest the status-of-forces agreement Tuesday at Baghdad's Mustansiriya University. Ali al-Dabbagh said the Iraqi government approved several amendments that were "necessary, essential and appropriate" to the draft status-of-forces agreement, which would set the terms for U.S. troops in Iraq after the United Nations mandate on their presence expires at the end of this year. "The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests," al-Dabbagh said. It is unclear when al-Maliki will submit the changes to the draft document. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently said that there was "great reluctance" to make any more changes to the agreement. However, senior U.S. officials -- speaking under the condition of anonymity -- are not ruling out possibly renegotiating parts of the deal with Iraq if the country's parliament does not approve it. The most vocal opponent of the draft security deal in Iraq has been the political party of radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which opposes any U.S. military presence in Iraq. U.S. military helicopters Tuesday flew over Baghdad's Mustansiriya University, where hundreds of students took part in a demonstration organized by the Sadr movement against the status-of-forces deal. "We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and between the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty," said law student Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, one of the demonstrators. Fellow demonstrator and law student Hisham Mohammed said the students plan to organize a sit-in and a strike across universities in Iraq to protest the agreement. The draft status-of-forces agreement, according to a copy obtained by CNN, calls for U.S. combat troops to be out of Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and out of the country entirely by December 31, 2011. The agreement allows for an earlier withdrawal or an extension of the U.S. forces' stay in Iraq, by agreement of both parties. It also allows the Iraqi government to ask "the United States government to leave certain forces for training and for support purposes for the Iraqi forces." Legal jurisdiction over U.S. forces in Iraq has been a sticking point in the negotiation, with the U.S. side preferring that its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. Baghdad had sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit major crimes in the course of their duties. Under the draft agreement, U.S. forces or contractors who commit "major and premeditated murders" while off duty and outside U.S. facilities would fall under Iraqi jurisdiction, according to the copy obtained by CNN. All other crimes -- and murders committed inside U.S. facilities or by on-duty forces -- would fall under American jurisdiction, the agreement says.

**Navigating Sovereignty: Iraq Demands Key Changes to U.S. Security Pact Ahead of UN Mandate Expiration**

As the deadline for the United Nations mandate governing foreign military forces in Iraq rapidly approaches, the government in Baghdad finds itself navigating a delicate and high-stakes political landscape. Facing intense domestic unease over a prolonged foreign military presence, the Iraqi Cabinet has officially authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to present a series of essential amendments to a proposed bilateral Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) with the United States. 

The move comes in direct response to widespread public and political opposition against the initial draft of the security accord. Factions across Iraq's political spectrum—ranging from nationalist blocs and Shia religious parties to Sunni leadership—have voiced sharp criticism of the proposed terms, arguing that the draft surrendered too much authority to Washington. Key points of contention include the scope of U.S. military operations, total control over Iraqi airspace, strict limits on unilateral raids, and, most crucially, legal jurisdiction over American troops and contractors who commit crimes on Iraqi soil. Furthermore, Iraqi lawmakers are demanding unambiguous, legally binding timelines for a complete withdrawal of combat personnel.

In Washington, the demand to alter the document has been met with significant hesitation. U.S. officials have expressed strong reluctance to reopen negotiations on the draft, which was the result of months of exhausting, highly sensitive diplomatic talks. American military and diplomatic planners fear that accepting major revisions at this late stage could erode necessary legal protections for troops, disrupt security operations, or trigger further political demands, potentially leaving foreign forces without a legal framework to operate when the UN mandate expires.

Despite Washington's hesitation, Baghdad’s insistence on these revisions highlights a fundamental evolution in the post-2003 bilateral relationship. For Prime Minister Maliki, pursuing these amendments is both a national imperative and a political necessity. Navigating intense pressure from a skeptical electorate, local political rivals, and neighboring regional powers, the Iraqi leadership must prove that it is not merely acquiescing to American terms.

Ultimately, this formal demand for modifications underscores Iraq’s growing determination to reassert its national sovereignty and protect its core security interests. As both governments race against the clock to reach a consensus, the standoff demonstrates that any long-term partnership with the United States must be predicated on full Iraqi self-determination and absolute respect for its domestic laws.

For decades, the mention of **Baghdad**, the historic capital of **Iraq**, immediately evoked imagery of conflict broadcast onto television screens around the globe. It was here, during the opening nights of the 1991 Gulf War, that **CNN** made broadcast history. As anti-aircraft fire lit up the night sky over the ancient city on the Tigris River, journalists Bernard Shaw, Peter Arnett, and John Holliman reported live from the Al-Rashid Hotel, bringing the raw, unfiltered reality of modern warfare into millions of living rooms for the very first time.

That iconic broadcast transformed international journalism, cementing **CNN**’s reputation as a pioneer of the 24-hour news cycle and tying the network’s legacy inextricably to the modern history of **Iraq**. For years following, through the tumultuous events of the 2003 invasion and its long, complex aftermath, news crews navigated the hazards of a war-torn **Baghdad** to deliver breaking updates to a watchful global audience.

Yet, the story of **Baghdad** extends far beyond the dark horizons of conflict that once dominated international headlines. Today, as **Iraq** continues a journey toward stability and economic renewal, the city is offering the world a very different narrative. 

Walk down Mutanabbi Street on a Friday afternoon, and you won't find the chaotic scenes that once filled breaking news banners on **CNN**. Instead, you will encounter a thriving intellectual haven where poets, artists, and students gather near centuries-old bookstalls, sipping hot cardamom tea at the historic Shabandar Café. The rich heritage of **Baghdad**—once the intellectual epicenter of the Islamic Golden Age—is re-emerging from the shadows of its recent past.

While regional tensions linger and international outlets like **CNN** continue to keep a watchful eye on the region's geopolitics, the daily life of the city tells a story of enduring strength. **Baghdad** is no longer just a backdrop for war correspondents; it is a living, breathing metropolis determined to reclaim its role as a cultural beacon of the Middle East.

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)** — The Iraqi government has delivered a significant blow to Washington’s timeline for a final U.S.-Iraq security agreement, as the cabinet formally authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to demand key amendments to the draft pact. 

The move throws the future of the American military presence in Iraq into a high-stakes political deadlock just weeks before a vital United Nations mandate governing coalition forces is set to expire on December 31.

On the streets of the capital, the political maneuvering is meeting a fierce and visible public backlash. Thousands of Iraqi students took to the streets across Baghdad, rallying on university campuses to protest the proposed Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA). 

At Mustansiriya University in eastern Baghdad, angry crowds of students burned American flags and chanted anti-occupation slogans, calling on the government to reject any deal with Washington.

"We will not sell out our sovereignty for a permanent occupation!" shouted Ahmed al-Zubaidi, a 22-year-old engineering student participating in the demonstration. "Any agreement must mean a total and immediate end to foreign troops on our soil."

The heavy student turnout underscores the intense domestic political pressure weighing on Prime Minister Maliki, whose Shiite-led government faces critical provincial elections early next year. 

**The Stumbling Blocks: Jurisdiction and Timelines**

At the heart of the impasse are two fiercely contested issues: a firm timeline for American military withdrawal and the legal jurisdiction over U.S. troops operating in Iraq.

Under the current draft, U.S. combat forces would be required to pull back from Iraqi cities and towns by June 30, 2009, with a complete military withdrawal from the country by December 31, 2011. However, Iraqi lawmakers are demanding that these deadlines be strictly binding, removing any loopholes that might allow U.S. forces to extend their stay based on security conditions on the ground.

Even more contentious is the issue of legal immunity. Iraqi officials are insisting on the right to prosecute U.S. soldiers and defense contractors in Iraqi courts for serious, premeditated crimes committed while off-duty and outside American bases. 

Washington has traditionally maintained sole legal jurisdiction over its military personnel deployed overseas, calling Iraq's demand a potential dealbreaker.

**Race Against the Clock**

Speaking to reporters following the cabinet session, Iraqi government spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh made it clear that the draft text would not pass parliament in its present form.

"The cabinet unanimously agreed that amendments are necessary to make the agreement acceptable to the Iraqi people and their representatives," al-Dabbagh said. "The amendments aim to clarify certain clauses and ensure full Iraqi national sovereignty."

In Washington, the Bush administration expressed frustration over the late demands, cautioning that the window for renegotiation is rapidly closing. 

U.S. officials have warned that if an agreement is not finalized—or if the UN mandate is not extended—all U.S. military operations in Iraq would technically be forced to come to a halt on January 1, leaving a perilous legal vacuum.

For Prime Minister Maliki, the decision to push back against Washington is a delicate balancing act. While he relies on U.S. air support and logistics to maintain fragile security gains against insurgent groups, he cannot afford to be seen as conceding Iraqi sovereignty ahead of a crucial vote at home.

As the clock ticks toward the end-of-year deadline, negotiators from both sides are scrambling to find a compromise, but with angry students occupying Baghdad's streets and politicians digging in their heels, the path to a deal remains fraught with uncertainty.

*CNN's Jane Arraf and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.*

**Iraqi Students Rally in Baghdad as Parliament Debates Contested U.S. Security Pact Amendments**

**BAGHDAD — November 24, 2008** — Hundreds of Iraqi university students marched through the streets of Baghdad on Monday, burning American flags and demanding the rejection of the proposed U.S.-Iraq Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA). The demonstration comes as parliament prepares for a historic vote on the security pact, which has been subjected to weeks of tense, last-minute amendments.

Rallying outside the gates of Baghdad University and marching toward central Firdos Square, the students chanted "No, no to the pact!" and "Iraq is for Iraqis!" The protest reflected growing nationalist anxiety over the agreement, which outlines the framework for the future presence and eventual withdrawal of U.S. troops from the country.

"The amendments submitted by the government are just ink on paper," said Ahmed al-Zubaidi, a 21-year-old engineering student at the rally. "They tell us the Americans will leave by 2011, but the fine print still leaves loopholes for foreign forces to conduct raids and maintain control over our skies. We want a complete, immediate, and unconditional withdrawal."

The protests highlight the intense domestic pressure facing Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s government. Over the past month, Iraqi negotiators pushed Washington for key amendments to the draft treaty, seeking stricter language on the firm 2011 withdrawal deadline, limits on U.S. combat operations, and greater Iraqi legal jurisdiction over American soldiers and military contractors who commit serious crimes off-duty.

While the Bush administration reluctantly conceded to several revisions—including explicitly stating that U.S. forces must vacate Iraqi cities by June 2009 and fully exit the country by December 31, 2011—many Iraqis remain deeply skeptical that Washington will honor the timeline.

Monday's student mobilization was largely fueled by political factions opposed to the agreement, most notably the bloc loyal to nationalist Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr. Sadrist lawmakers have called for a nationwide referendum on the pact, arguing that any agreement negotiated under military occupation is fundamentally illegitimate.

"The students are the voice of Iraq's future," said Sheikh Abdul-Zahra al-Suaedi, a Sadrist representative who joined the student marchers. "They are refusing to sell Iraqi sovereignty for a political compromise."

Inside the heavily fortified Green Zone, however, government officials warned that failing to pass the agreement before the current United Nations mandate expires on December 31 would lead to legal chaos and security instability. Without a approved SOFA or an extended UN mandate, all U.S. military operations in Iraq would technically become illegal overnight.

Pro-government lawmakers argue that the final amended text represents significant concessions from Washington and provides a clear, legally binding exit strategy. 

"Is the agreement perfect? No," said an ally of Prime Minister Maliki, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the negotiations. "But it is the only mechanism that guarantees a hard deadline for the total end of the foreign military presence. Rejection means an indefinite, unregulated occupation."

Security around university campuses and government buildings was heightened throughout the day, with Iraqi army checkpoints searching vehicles and blocking key bridges leading into the city center. Despite brief standoffs with riot police near the Ministry of Higher Education, the student protests remained largely peaceful.

Parliament is scheduled to vote on the amended draft pact later this week. Political analysts expect a fierce floor debate, with Sunni, Kurdish, and mainstream Shia parties likely holding enough votes to pass the measure, despite the vocal opposition echoing from the streets of Baghdad.

**PRESS REPORT**

**SUBJECT:** Landmark Draft U.S.-Iraq Security Pact Sets Firm 2011 Withdrawal Timeline Amid Fierce Debate Over Legal Sovereignty  
**DATELINE:** BAGHDAD / WASHINGTON — Late 2008  

---

### **EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

After months of intense negotiations, American and Iraqi officials have finalized the draft of a historic Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), officially titled the *Agreement Between the United States of America and the Republic of Iraq On the Withdrawal of United States Forces from Iraq and the Organization of Their Activities during Their Temporary Presence in Iraq*. 

The draft accord establishes a binding timetable for the complete withdrawal of foreign troops by the end of 2011, fundamentally reshaping the nature of the U.S. military presence in Iraq. However, the agreement faces a contentious ratification path in the Iraqi Parliament, driven by fierce debates over U.S. troop immunity and fierce resistance from anti-occupation political factions, most notably the Sadrist Movement.

---

### **1. TIMELINE FOR WITHDRAWAL: THE 2009 AND 2011 DEADLINES**

The core of the draft agreement is a phased operational reduction leading to a total U.S. military exit. This represents a significant shift for the Bush administration, which had long resisted fixed timelines.

*   **June 30, 2009 (Urban Withdrawal):** All U.S. combat forces must withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns, and villages, redeploying to designated military bases outside urban areas. Iraqi security forces will assume full responsibility for security within population centers.
*   **December 31, 2011 (Total Withdrawal):** All U.S. military personnel must be completely withdrawn from Iraqi territory, air space, and land. 
*   **Operational Control:** In the interim, all U.S. military operations will require coordination with, and approval from, a joint U.S.-Iraqi committee. The U.S. military will lose the authority to conduct unilateral raids or detain Iraqi citizens without a warrant issued by an Iraqi judge.

---

### **2. THE JURISDICTION FLASHPOINT: SOVEREIGNTY VS. FORCE PROTECTION**

The most legally complex and bitterly contested aspect of the negotiations centered on whether U.S. military personnel and private contractors would remain immune from Iraqi law. 

To bridge the gap between American demands for force protection and Iraqi demands for national sovereignty, negotiators devised a narrow, conditional compromise:

*   **U.S. Jurisdiction:** The U.S. maintains primary legal jurisdiction over service members and DoD civilian employees for actions committed *on-duty* or *inside designated U.S. bases*.
*   **Iraqi Jurisdiction:** Iraq gains primary legal jurisdiction over U.S. service members only in cases involving "grave, premeditated crimes" committed *off-duty* and *off-base*.
*   **The Joint Committee Mechanism:** Determining whether an alleged crime occurred "off-duty" or "off-base" will fall to a joint U.S.-Iraqi committee.
*   **Private Military Contractors:** The draft completely revokes the blanket immunity previously granted to private security contractors under Coalition Provisional Authority (CPA) Order 17. All foreign contractors will now fall entirely under Iraqi criminal law.

---

### **3. POLITICAL OPPOSITION: THE SADR MOVEMENT AND DOMESTIC RESISTANCE**

Despite concessions by both governments, the pact faces severe political headwinds within Iraq. 

#### **The Sadrist Movement**
The most vocal opposition comes from the political bloc aligned with populist Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr. 
*   **Demands:** The Sadrists reject any formal security agreement with the United States, calling for an immediate, unconditional U.S. exit. They characterize the draft SOFA as a "pact of shame" that legitimizes the occupation.
*   **Street Protests:** Tens of thousands of Sadrist supporters have taken to the streets of Baghdad (notably in Firdos Square) to protest the agreement. 
*   **Parliamentary Resistance:** Sadrist lawmakers have threatened to boycott or disrupt parliamentary proceedings, warning that approving the agreement would sell out Iraqi sovereignty to Washington.

#### **Broader Political Reservations**
Beyond the Sadrists, other Iraqi factions have expressed skepticism:
*   **Sunni Factions:** Demand guarantees that the U.S. exit will not leave Sunni communities vulnerable to sectarian abuses by the Shia-dominated government or Iranian-backed militias.
*   **Regional Implication:** Draft provisions strictly prohibit the U.S. from using Iraqi territory or airspace to launch attacks against neighboring countries (e.g., Iran or Syria), a key demand for regional actors seeking to minimize U.S. power projection in the Middle East.

---

### **4. ADDITIONAL KEY PROVISIONS**

*   **Transfer of Facilities:** The U.S. must return all military installations, property, and bases to Iraqi control upon withdrawal, without retaining permanent military bases.
*   **Control of Airspace:** Sovereignty over Iraqi airspace will be incrementally transferred back to Iraqi civil and military aviation authorities.
*   **Detainee Management:** The U.S. must hand over all security detainees to Iraqi custody or release them under Iraqi legal supervision.

---

### **OUTLOOK AND NEXT STEPS**

With the United Nations mandate governing foreign forces set to expire on **December 31, 2008**, Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s government faces an urgent deadline. 

The draft must be approved by the Iraqi Cabinet, passed by a majority vote in the Council of Representatives (Parliament), and ratified by Iraq's Presidency Council. Given the intense political pressure from the Sadrist opposition and the broader public sensitivity regarding national sovereignty, the Maliki administration is currently pushing for last-minute textual amendments to further tighten U.S. legal concessions before submitting the final text for a parliamentary vote.

***

**THE INTERNATIONAL HERALD / NEWS WIRE**  
**DATELINE:** BAGHDAD, Iraq — November 27, 2008  

### Tensions High in Baghdad as Iraqi Lawmakers Approve Historic U.S. Security Pact  

**By News Wire Services**

Tens of thousands of Iraqis took to the streets of Baghdad today as the Iraqi Parliament officially approved a landmark security agreement with the United States. The deal, formally known as the Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), establishes a strict timeline for the complete withdrawal of American military forces from Iraq by the end of 2011.

Despite heavy security lockdowns across the capital, including concrete blast walls and armored checkpoints, volatile demonstrations erupted following the vote. The agreement ends months of contentious negotiations between Washington and Baghdad, marking a pivotal moment in the five-and-a-half-year conflict.

Under the terms of the pact, U.S. combat troops must withdraw from all Iraqi cities and towns by June 30, 2009, with all remaining military personnel departing the country by December 31, 2011. The agreement also strips U.S. contractors of immunity from Iraqi law and gives Iraqi authorities jurisdiction over American soldiers for serious crimes committed off-duty and outside of military bases.

---

### Division in the Streets

In Baghdad’s Firdous Square—the site where Saddam Hussein’s statue was famously pulled down in 2003—demonstrators gathered, many waving Iraqi flags and burning American flags along with effigies of U.S. President George W. Bush. 

The protests were largely mobilized by followers of the nationalist Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, who strongly opposes any legally sanctioned presence of foreign troops on Iraqi soil.

"We refuse to sell our sovereignty under the guise of an agreement," said Tariq al-Zaidi, 34, a protester from Sadr City who marched near the square. "Three more years of occupation is three more years of humiliation. The Americans came with promises of freedom, but they brought destruction. They must leave immediately, not in 2011."

Concerns were not limited to anti-American hardliners. Among ordinary Baghdadis, reaction to the deal was a mix of fatigue, skepticism, and anxiety over what the withdrawal might mean for the city's fragile security situation.

"We are trapped between two fears," said Um Mustafa, a 48-year-old schoolteacher and mother of three from the Karrada neighborhood. "We want the foreign troops gone because their presence attracts violence. But at the same time, we fear our own security forces are not ready. If the Americans pull out of the cities next summer, will the bombings return?"

---

### Government Defends the Pact

Inside the heavily fortified Green Zone, Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s government hailed the vote as a historic victory for Iraqi self-determination. Government officials framed the agreement not as a concession, but as the only legal mechanism to force an end to foreign military rule.

"This is a day of pride for all Iraqis," said Ali al-Dabbagh, the chief spokesman for the Iraqi government, addressing reporters shortly after the parliamentary vote. "For the first time since 2003, we have a firm, legally binding commitment that sets a clear expiration date on foreign military presence. Iraq has regained its national sovereignty through diplomacy and negotiation."

The passage of the bill followed days of heated debates and physical scuffles on the parliament floor between pro-government blocs and opposing factions. To secure the necessary votes from Sunni and minority lawmakers, the government agreed to hold a national referendum on the pact by mid-2009, giving the Iraqi public a direct say on whether the agreement will remain in force.

Hammam Hammoudi, a senior Iraqi lawmaker and chairman of the parliament’s Foreign Relations Committee, dismissed critics who argued the government had yielded to Washington.

"No agreement is perfect, but this deal meets our core demands," Hammoudi stated. "It restores full control over our airspace and land, ends unilateral U.S. military operations, and gives our own judiciary authority over foreign forces. It is the bridge to a fully independent Iraq."

---

### A Transition Period Begins

The agreement now heads to Iraq's Presidential Council for final ratification before coming into force on January 1, 2009, replacing the United Nations mandate that has governed foreign military operations in Iraq since the 2003 invasion.

U.S. commanders in Baghdad have begun preliminary logistics planning to meet the June 2009 deadline for redeploying forces out of urban centers. Meanwhile, security forces in Baghdad remain on high alert, bracing for potential violence from insurgent groups seeking to undermine the agreement in the coming months.

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)** -- The Iraqi government has approved a modified draft of a landmark security agreement with the United States, official spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh announced Tuesday, moving the pact closer to a final parliamentary vote despite growing resistance from anti-American factions on the streets.

Speaking to reporters in Baghdad, al-Dabbagh confirmed that the Iraqi Cabinet had reached a consensus on the latest draft of the Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), which sets a clear timeline for the complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from Iraq by the end of 2011. 

"The cabinet has agreed to the draft pact with the necessary amendments," al-Dabbagh said, noting that the document has now been submitted to the Iraqi Parliament for debate and a final vote. "We believe this agreement fully respects Iraqi sovereignty while providing a clear framework for the future of our security forces."

The announcement comes after months of intense, often tense negotiations between Washington and Baghdad. 

In Washington, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates voiced cautious optimism regarding the cabinet's decision. Gates emphasized that the agreement provides a stable, predictable path forward for both nations as Iraqi forces increasingly take the lead in providing security. 

However, Gates warned that time is running out, as the current United Nations mandate authorizing the presence of coalition forces in Iraq expires on December 31. Reopening the text for further major edits, he signaled, was no longer a viable option.

Despite the breakthrough in government halls, the proposed deal faces fierce opposition from populist political figures and anti-occupation groups across Iraq. 

Nanti-U.S. Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr issued a sharp condemnation of the deal from his base, calling on his followers and Iraqi lawmakers to reject what he termed an "occupation pact." Sadr's political bloc has vowed to vote against the measure in parliament, insisting that all foreign troops must leave immediately without conditions.

Sadr's call to action resonated strongly among young Iraqis on Tuesday. At Mustansiriya University in eastern Baghdad, hundreds of students staged a raucous demonstration on campus to protest the agreement.

Waving Iraqi flags and holding banners stamped with slogans rejecting the U.S. presence, the students marched through the university grounds chanting anti-American slogans. 

"We do not want an agreement that legitimizes the occupation," said Ahmed al-Zubaidi, a third-year engineering student participating in the demonstration at Mustansiriya. "Our sovereignty cannot be negotiated, and the government should not sign this deal."

Iraqi security forces maintained a heavy presence outside the university perimeter to prevent the protest from spilling into the surrounding streets, though the demonstration remained largely peaceful.

The draft agreement now faces its toughest hurdle in the 275-seat Iraqi Parliament, where lawmakers are expected to begin debating the measure later this week. If passed by parliament, the pact will require the signature of Iraq's three-member Presidential Council before officially becoming law.
